note: Every claim below cites a section of the specification and either reads
that section's own enumerations out of the document at run time, or runs a
program the section's text implies. `ggc conform` is the runner; see
conformance/README.md. A claim whose expectation is wrong fails loudly,
and a claim about the toolkit failing to meet the document is either a
failure or an entry in deviations.json -- never silence.

claims.claim: every type name section 5 lists can be used as written
claims.why: Section 5 lists the primitive, compound and domain types by name. Reading that list out of the document and declaring a parameter of each is the difference between checking the specification and checking the compiler's own idea of what it implements.

claims.claim: every compilation stage is implemented or explained
claims.why: Section 22 names fourteen stages. Each is either performed by a named part of this compiler, or recorded as not implemented with a reason; a stage that is neither is a silent gap.

claims.claim: every v1.0 requirement is evidenced or not claimed
claims.why: Section 33 is what stops a release from claiming more than it has. Each of its twenty items has to be answered -- with a command a reader can run, or with an explicit refusal to claim -- and an item that disappears from the checklist is a failure.

claims.claim: the syntax section's own examples are accepted and mean what they say
`let` is immutable, so assigning to one is refused
adding Text to I64 is a compile-time diagnostic, not a runtime surprise
a `pure` function that writes a file is refused for that reason
a program that reads a file without the capability does not read it
a secret cannot be printed through ordinary output
an error that is not a defect travels as a Result value
an unrecoverable defect stops the program with a named fault
a function that declares `deterministic` gives the same answer twice
the same source compiles to the same output twice
